evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 下 as an indicative graph: the Shang oracle-bone form places a short stroke below a longer reference stroke, expressing the lower position. It reports that the curved reference line was later commonly written as a horizontal line; early oracle-bone and bronze forms are identified as 𠄟. The entry says a vertical stroke was added in late Spring and Autumn forms to distinguish it from 上 and 二, and that Warring States regional forms no longer used 𠄟. Chu forms may add a short decorative stroke above. This conflicts in detail with the Academia Sinica account, which describes the reference as a horizon and puts the distinguishing change in small seal writing.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 下

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.field: 甲骨文 / bronze and transmitted-text uses
evidence.text: The entry cites oracle-bone 《合集》7428「下上若(諾)，受(授)我又(祐)」, interpreted as the agreement of lower deities and upper deities, and 《屯南》1115「下示五牢」, a sacrifice to the lower ancestral spirits. For bronze inscriptions it cites 番生𣪕蓋「廣啟厥孫子于下」 as 下 referring to the human world below, and records 下官 as an office and 下淢 as a place name. It describes later transmitted uses for humility toward a superior, then the verb sense ‘descend’, with ‘capture/take (a city)’ exemplified by 《戰國策·齊策六》「唯莒、即墨不下」. These attestations show multiple uses but do not establish a complete dated semantic sequence.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 下

evidence.source: 中央研究院文字學資料庫 / Academia Sinica Character Database
evidence.text: The graph-history note says the oracle-bone form has two horizontal strokes: the longer upper stroke represents the horizon and the shorter lower stroke is an indicative mark for ‘below’. It says a different 下 form arose in small seal script to avoid confusion with 二, changing the lower horizontal stroke to a vertical stroke. The page lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu bamboo-and-silk, small-seal, and Shuowen-seal sections, but its machine-readable text does not identify a dated specimen for each stage.
evidence.title: 漢字「下」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.text: The database gives the received Shuowen entry as 「丅，底也。指事。下，篆文丅。」 (‘丅: bottom; indicative. 下 is the seal-script form of 丅’), and notes that Duan Yucai emended the Shuowen headword’s ancient form to 𠄟. This is an early lexicographic analysis, not direct confirmation of the Shang graph’s shape or date.

evidence.text: The database describes the oracle-bone form as two horizontal strokes: the upper, longer line represents the horizon and the lower, shorter line is an indicative mark for ‘below’. It says a small-seal form changed the lower horizontal to a vertical stroke to avoid confusion with 二. This account is not fully aligned with CUHK’s placement of the added vertical stroke in late Spring and Autumn forms.

evidence.text: The entry quotes the received Shuowen explanation: 「丅，底也。指事。下，篆文丅。」 It interprets the oracle graph as a short stroke placed below a curved line, later often made horizontal; it says late Spring and Autumn forms commonly added a vertical stroke to avoid confusion with 上 and 二. It cites oracle-bone uses 《合集》7428 and 《屯南》1115, bronze uses including 番生𣪕蓋, and later extensions to humility, ‘descend’, and ‘capture/take’ (《戰國策·齊策六》). These examples show uses, but the entry does not provide a complete dated semantic sequence.

No phonetic component is proposed for 下 by the inspected sources; hence there is no component pronunciation comparison to report. Modern xià is sourced from the local Unihan row and Unicode sources, and historical readings are reported only for the host character.

Graphic chronology differs between sources: CUHK says the added vertical stroke appears commonly in late Spring and Autumn and discusses distinguishing 上 and 二; Academia Sinica associates the changed form with small seal script and specifically mentions confusion with 二. Precise transition dates and individual dated exemplars need specialist specimen-level verification.

The cited bronze and transmitted-text examples are presented with inscription identifiers but not independently checked against photographs, editions, or archaeological dates in this pass. The semantic extensions from ‘below’ to ‘descend’, ‘inferior’, humility, and ‘capture’ are not all dated by those sources.

The dossier’s Proto-Sino-Tibetan versus Austroasiatic word-origin proposals and proposed cognates were not independently researched in this bounded pass; those concern the spoken word’s etymology, not the independently supported graphic formation.

The local Baxter–Sagart rows are present in the supplied data, but an inspectable character-specific upstream edition/table source could not be verified. Zhengzhang forms and cross-system equivalence were not independently audited.

The precise chronology of the lower stroke's change to a vertical remains disputed: Academia Sinica associates it with small seal script, while CUHK says it was common in late Spring and Autumn forms. Specimen-level dates were not verified.

The inscription identifiers and semantic examples are reported by CUHK but were not independently checked against inscription photographs or dated editions. The sources do not establish a complete chronology for extensions from ‘below’ to ‘descend’, humility, or ‘capture’.
